# Multi-Agent Financial Analysis System
**AAI-520 Final Team Project**  
**Tim Hays · Roopleen Kaur · Ashley Marx**  
[GitHub repository](https://github.com/tim17hays/NLP_AAI520) · [Project source](https://github.com/tim17hays/NLP_AAI520/tree/codex/final-team-integration)

This project integrates research planning, specialist tools, financial news analysis, output evaluation and persistent memory into an investment-research workflow. The system retrieves source-attributed evidence, produces an analysis, evaluates its quality and retains reusable process lessons.

The report presents an AAPL case study and controlled DEMO experiments. The controlled comparison examines how a stored lesson changes drafting behavior under identical inputs. Language-model judgments and arithmetic/citation verification are reported separately. The analyses are educational research examples, not investment recommendations.

## 1. System architecture and team contributions
| Capability | Implementation | Demonstration |
|---|---|---|
| Research planning | `ResearchPlanner.plan()` | Ordered research steps and specialist selection |
| Tool use | Question-dependent tool selection | Market, earnings, news and company routes; AAPL evidence trace |
| Self-reflection | Qwen review with citation and content checks | Criterion scores, feedback and re-evaluation |
| Persistent memory | Process lessons stored in JSON | Disk persistence, retrieval before planning and memory-controlled drafting |
| News chaining | Ingest → preprocess → classify → extract → summarize | Stage trace, deduplication, FinBERT inference and source alignment |
| Specialist routing | Market, earnings, news and company specialists | Different research questions select different tools |
| Evaluator–optimizer | Review → evidence-bound revision → re-evaluation | Original and revised analyses with evidence verification |

Tim contributed retrieval, news processing and integration; Roopleen contributed planning, specialist routing and initial draft generation; Ashley contributed evaluation, revision and persistent memory. Component implementations and experiment provenance are retained in the repository.

The architecture combines LLM judgment with deterministic routing and arithmetic. Routing uses research-question keywords. Retrieved lessons activate an auditable drafting policy without changing model weights. The numeric report compiler requires compatible inputs, explicit units and reporting periods.

## 2. Models and reproducibility
The original generation/review model is `Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct`. The CPU review experiment uses `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`, and news sentiment uses `ProsusAI/finbert`. Models run through Hugging Face Transformers. Optional Finnhub and Alpha Vantage credentials are kept outside the repository.

Recorded experiments include model identities, software versions, timestamps, source fingerprints and raw judgments. Report execution validates and presents those records; it is distinct from performing new inference. The loader supports CUDA, Apple MPS and CPU.

Experiment entry points are `scripts/run_grounded_demo.py` and `scripts/run_finbert_demo.py`. Each research experiment uses a separate directory to isolate memory. `AAI520_DEVICE`, `AAI520_MODEL_NAME` and `AAI520_MODEL_PATH` identify the selected device and model snapshot.

## 3. News processing and source validation
The news chain ingests records, normalizes text and URLs, removes duplicates, classifies retained text with FinBERT, extracts source sentences and produces a source-preserving summary. Each stage records its inputs or outputs.

Deterministic classifier fixtures isolate provenance and error-handling behavior. The FinBERT experiment separately demonstrates actual model inference on explicitly fictional classroom news. Classification confidence describes the model's sentiment judgment, not the truth of a report or the probability of a stock-price movement.

Yahoo news requests use a 20-second timeout and a 15-minute successful-result cache. The fallback sequence is Yahoo → Finnhub → Alpha Vantage. Historical-price requests use a 15-second timeout.
final-10: These checks verify deduplication, alignment between extracted sentences and retained source text, and handling of unavailable provider or classifier responses. Provider access times are distinguished from financial reporting periods.

### FinBERT experiment
The production `NewsPipeline` processes duplicated fictional news with the actual `ProsusAI/finbert` model. The displayed trace records all five stages, duplicate removal and source alignment. This experiment demonstrates execution and provenance rather than sentiment-accuracy benchmarking.

The planner selects specialists from research-question keywords and returns evidence, an ordered plan, a tool trace, retrieved lessons and a draft. Questions without a matching specialist use the company-profile route. The examples below illustrate specialist selection and incorporation of a process lesson into planning.

### AAPL case study
The AAPL case study uses the recorded Colab execution associated with commit `34dbce9`. Source URLs, access times, missing fields and provider diagnostics accompany the retrieved market, financial and news evidence. The fixed DEMO benchmark is examined separately to control the inputs used in the memory comparison.

## 5. Evaluation, revision and persistent memory
The evaluator assigns 0–2 points for evidence support, completeness, consistency, uncertainty and clarity. Acceptance requires at least 8/10, no zero-valued criterion, full evidence support and consistency, and no critical issues. Citation checks validate supplied references; benchmark checks examine selected computed facts.

Revision stops on acceptance, at the two-revision limit or when a proposed draft is unchanged. Memory retains reusable process lessons rather than current prices or predictions. Duplicate lessons reuse the existing record.

The model transport permits one additional attempt for an invalid JSON/schema response. Original responses and validation diagnostics are retained. Formatting retries are distinct from analysis revisions.
final-18:
### Controlled inputs and software validation
DEMO is a fictional classroom company. Its figures, dates, news and `example.com` URLs are synthetic. The supplied inputs imply 20% revenue growth, 10% operating margin and 10% closing-price change. No prior operating-income comparison, guaranteed return or price target is supplied.

Scripted tests validate interfaces, arithmetic safeguards, citation handling, memory persistence and stopping rules. Real-model experiment records are presented separately.

## 6. Baseline experiment
The Colab baseline uses fixed fictional DEMO evidence. Run 1 begins with an uncited benchmark draft, and Run 2 uses Qwen generation with a retrieved process lesson. Evaluation histories, model scores and reference checks are retained.

Because the initial drafts have different origins, baseline score differences do not isolate a memory effect. Section 8 instead compares the same raw candidate and evidence with and without the stored drafting policy.
final-22:
## 7. Baseline results
The results below identify the experiment source and show initial and final scores, revisions, acceptance decisions and lessons received. Drafts and evaluation histories provide the supporting detail for the comparison.
final-24:
### Interpretation of the baseline
Run 1 received 7/10 before and after two revisions. Run 2 received 6/10 and terminated when its proposed revision was unchanged. Both remained below the configured acceptance conditions, while lesson persistence and delivery checks were satisfied.

The baseline illustrates two distinct evaluation concerns: references can be omitted even when calculations are correct, and a retrieved lesson does not by itself ensure consistent numerical statements. The supplied inputs establish **20% revenue growth, 10% operating margin and 10% closing-price change**.

The evidence-bound policy addresses these concerns by calculating metrics from supplied inputs and placing valid references alongside claims. Model acceptance and independent evidence verification remain separate measurements throughout the subsequent experiment.
grounded-introduction:
## 8. Evidence-bound optimization and memory comparison
This experiment holds a previously generated Qwen candidate and its fictional evidence fixed. `ResearchPlanner` selects dataset-backed market, earnings and news tools. The evaluation loop receives real model judgments, and a deterministic evidence tool constructs a cited analytical brief.

In Run 1, evaluation identifies issues in the original candidate, the optimizer constructs a brief, and the new candidate is re-evaluated and checked against the supplied evidence. A process lesson is stored on disk. In Run 2, that record is retrieved before planning and drafting and activates the evidence-bound policy before evaluation.

The CPU reviewer assigns each criterion separately using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. The original Colab baseline used Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, so their scores are not treated as a controlled comparison between models. The same-input policy comparison measures the effect of the stored drafting policy independently of the reviewer change.

The compiler reads evidence fields, units, periods and formulas rather than a reference answer. Changed-input tests check that calculations follow the data. Incomplete inputs and unresolved snapshot errors are rejected.
grounded-scope:
### Interpretation and scope
Both evidence-bound briefs contain the supplied metrics with compatible periods and valid references. Independent checks confirm 20% revenue growth, 10% operating margin and 10% closing-price change. News is attributed to its supplied source, and price change is distinguished from total return.

The same-input comparison shows that the stored lesson activates a policy that addresses the measured citation and calculation issues before the second draft is evaluated. Model acceptance decisions remain as recorded and are distinct from these evidence checks.

The compiler supports a defined numeric-snapshot schema. These findings describe the controlled example and do not establish general financial accuracy, predictive investment value or changes to model weights.
final-26:
## 9. Conclusions
The system integrates research planning, specialist tool use, self-reflection and persistent memory with news chaining, routing and evaluator–optimizer workflows. Source traces connect retrieved records to analysis, while evaluation histories document review and revision behavior.

The controlled comparison demonstrates a concrete use of retained state: a stored process lesson changes drafting policy before the subsequent analysis. Under identical inputs, the evidence-bound policy improves the measured calculation and citation checks. Recorded model judgments remain a separate quality signal.

The AAPL case study demonstrates provider integration, and the fictional benchmark isolates arithmetic and memory behavior. Together, the experiments illustrate how retrieval, model review, deterministic verification and persistent notes can be combined in an auditable research system.

## 10. AI assistance disclosure and responsibility
OpenAI Codex assisted with code development and debugging, retrieval reliability, repository integration, evaluation and revision interfaces, model-response formatting, evidence-bound reporting, memory-policy demonstrations, regression tests, notebook assembly, narrative editing and export validation. The report documents the resulting implementation, tests and limitations and distinguishes AI-generated material from independently verified evidence.

The team's primary contributions remain attributed throughout the notebook and Git history. Ashley's component notebook includes her own AI-use disclosure. Recorded model runs retain their actual runtime and provenance. Tool-generated briefs, model judgments, source quotations and scripted test fixtures are labeled separately.

The evidence brief uses deterministic arithmetic and source-bound wording to maintain arithmetic consistency and source attribution; it is not presented as an LLM-generated improvement. Team members remain responsible for understanding, validating, explaining and submitting the work.
